original_question: For the cubic family x' = ax + by, y' = cx^3 + dx^2 y + ex y^2 + fy^3, determine whether 2 is the maximum possible number of limit cycles; and for the more concrete equation x' = y, y' = -x^3 + dx^2 y + y^3, determine whether the limit cycle, when it exists, is unique and give a simple proof of that fact if it is true.
target_in_paper: Section 2.2, Problem 3(i)–(ii) ('Systems with homogeneous components'), introduced as the first challenge in the n = 1, m = 3 case of Problem 2 after Theorem 2.1. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper: it preserves the two-part structure of the official problem, gives the exact cubic family in Problem 3(i), singles out the exact concrete subfamily in Problem 3(ii), and asks precisely about the candidate upper bound 2 and the uniqueness/simple-proof issue. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))
missing_details: The paper is working in the real planar setting: the coefficients/parameters are real, the independent variable is real time t, and 'limit cycle' means an isolated periodic orbit in R^2. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))

The family in part (i) is not an arbitrary cubic planar vector field; it is the degree-(1,3) homogeneous-components family dx/dt = P1(x,y), dy/dt = Q3(x,y), where P1 is homogeneous of degree 1 and Q3 is homogeneous of degree 3. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))

The number 2 is not arbitrary: it comes from Theorem 2.1 and Problem 2, which ask whether (n+m)/2 is the maximal number of limit cycles for odd homogeneous degrees n != m; Problem 3(i) is exactly the specialization n = 1, m = 3, so (n+m)/2 = 2. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))

In part (i), 'maximum number' means the maximum over all real choices of the parameters a,b,c,d,e,f in that family, not for one fixed parameter tuple. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))

Part (ii) is the one-parameter subfamily obtained by fixing a = 0, b = 1, c = -1, e = 0, f = 1, leaving only the real parameter d free. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))

The phrase 'when it exists' in part (ii) should be read globally in the parameter d: the paper asks whether the concrete system can ever have more than one limit cycle, not just whether uniqueness holds in the already-proved parameter ranges. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))

Nearby context gives the currently known partial information for the concrete system: no limit cycles for d >= 0 or d < -2.679; at most one for -2.381 < d < 0; at least one for -2.110 < d < 0; and numerically the existence interval appears to shrink to about -2.198 < d < 0. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))

The request for a 'simple proof' is motivated by the surrounding Bendixson-Dulac framework: the paper notes that the first two partial results for the concrete system are obtained via suitable Dulac functions, and Theorem 2.2 is the nearby tool highlighted for such uniqueness questions. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))

No nilpotency, complex-field, or formal-series hypothesis is involved here; the paper’s critical structural restrictions are real planar dynamics and homogeneity of degrees 1 and 3. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))
refined_question: For real planar polynomial differential systems with homogeneous components of degrees 1 and 3, namely dx/dt = ax + by and dy/dt = cx^3 + dx^2y + exy^2 + fy^3 with a,b,c,d,e,f in R, is the maximum possible number of limit cycles (isolated periodic orbits in R^2) equal to 2? More concretely, for the one-parameter subfamily obtained by a = 0, b = 1, c = -1, e = 0, f = 1, namely dx/dt = y and dy/dt = -x^3 + d x^2 y + y^3 with d in R, is there at most one limit cycle whenever a limit cycle exists, and, if so, can this uniqueness be proved by a simple argument? ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))
justification: The closest paper-faithful target is Section 2.2, Problem 3(i)–(ii), not the broader neighboring problems in other sections. Theorem 2.1 and Problem 2 supply the hidden structure behind your draft—homogeneous components of odd degrees 1 and 3 and the candidate bound (n+m)/2 = 2—while the paragraph immediately after Problem 3 and the nearby Theorem 2.2 explain why the paper also isolates the subfamily dx/dt = y, dy/dt = -x^3 + d x^2 y + y^3 and asks for a simple uniqueness proof. ([ddd.uab.cat](https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2021/257127/semajou_a2021v78n3p233.pdf))
